segments.voice: Yesterday, Nandini: Vasishtha's cow, a curse he couldn't unsay, and why the eighth son had to live. Did you add a better word after one you couldn't take back? Day seven hundred eight.

The Ganga has gone shallow. Shantanu notices it while he's out hunting, following a wounded deer along the bank. The great river is barely moving, as if something upstream were holding it back. Ganga left him long ago, carrying their baby into the water, and he has ruled alone since then. Now he forgets the deer and goes looking for the reason instead, to find out what on earth could stop it.
screen: `THE RIVER HAS GONE SHALLOW.` → `THE KING LEAVES THE DEER.` → `WHAT COULD STOP A RIVER?`

segments.voice: By the water he finds a young man, tall and handsome, standing at the water's edge. He has stopped the Ganga's flow with arrows, a dam of them across the current. Shantanu has never seen anything like it. And he has no idea who this is. The young man sees the king, and with a power of illusion he clouds the king's senses and vanishes. So Shantanu is left on the bank with a suspicion. Could that have been my son? He calls on Ganga: show me the child. And she rises from the river in a beautiful form, holding the young man by the hand. This, she tells him, is your eighth son, the one I took with me. The text knows him by two names: Devavrata, and Gangeya, Ganga's son. Now look at the order the scene is told in. Shantanu sees what this young man can do before he knows who he is. He watches a stranger hold back a river. He loses him. And then he has to be introduced to his own child by the boy's mother. The son grew up out of his father's sight. When they finally meet, the father has to start where anyone would, with a name and a question. Some readers hear in the dam of arrows a first look at the strength this son will carry through the whole long poem. For now, a king who lost eight sons is standing beside one of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devavrata: a river held back by arrows, and a father introduced to his own son. What did you ask someone close? Day seven hundred nine.

Vasishtha. Ushanas. Brihaspati. Rama, the son of Jamadagni. That's the list Ganga gives the king. She's standing before Shantanu at the river's edge, holding their grown son by the hand, and before she lets go of him she tells his father what the boy has learned while he was away, and whose learning he holds. It's an extraordinary list. And the first name on it is the one that should make us stop.
screen: `A LIST OF TEACHERS.` → `SPOKEN AT THE RIVER'S EDGE.` → `THE FIRST NAME.`

segments.voice: He studied the Vedas, Ganga says, with Vasishtha. Two days ago we heard that name. Vasishtha is the sage whose cow was stolen, who cursed the Vasus, and who said the one who took her would live long on earth. The one who took her was Dyu. And Dyu is this young man. So the sage who sentenced him to a human life is the one who taught him how to live it. Then the list goes on. He knows, Ganga says, everything Ushanas knows, the teacher the asuras follow, and everything Brihaspati knows, the teacher of the gods. And he knows every weapon known to Rama, the son of Jamadagni, the warrior sage tradition calls Parashurama. Take him home, she says. And she goes back into the water, and this time she doesn't return to the story for a long while. Shantanu brings his son to the capital and makes him heir to the throne, and the text says the people of the kingdom are glad of him. Now step back, because this is the last day of Shantanu and Ganga, and the pieces fit. A king stared in heaven, and was born on earth to meet the river. Gods stole a cow, and were born to leave as fast as they came. A vow made by a riverbank kept a father silent seven times. And the one who broke the vow saved the one son who was always meant to stay. One Vasu remains on earth, taught by the sage who cursed him, heir to a throne, and marked, by that same curse, to have no children. The next turn of the story asks what that long life will cost him.

710.title: Bhishma's vow
710.carry: the no and the longing, side by side
710.howItsDone: In some Hindu marriages the families meet and talk before a match is agreed, and in some weddings the bride's father gives his daughter in a rite called kanyadana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gangeya: a son taught by the sage who cursed him, brought home as heir. Who did you thank for something they taught you? Day seven hundred ten.

A scent on the wind, sweet and strong, out by the Yamuna River. King Shantanu is walking in the woods along the bank when he catches it, and he can't tell where it comes from. So he follows it. It leads him to the water, and to a young woman with a boat, who ferries travelers across. He asks who she is. She's the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she says, and she plies this boat at her father's bidding.
screen: `A SCENT BY THE YAMUNA.` → `THE KING FOLLOWS IT.` → `A YOUNG WOMAN WITH A BOAT.`

segments.voice: Shantanu wants to marry her. He goes to her father and asks. The fisherman doesn't refuse. He says his daughter must marry someday, and the king is welcome. But there's a condition. Promise me, he says, that the son born of her will be king after you. And Shantanu can't. He already has an heir: Devavrata, Ganga's son, the young man he brought home from the river and made heir to the throne. To promise the crown to a son not yet born would mean taking it from the son he has. So the king says nothing to the fisherman's condition, and goes home. That should be the end of it. It isn't. Back in the capital, Shantanu can't stop thinking about her. He grows quiet and withdrawn, sunk in thought, the text says, and he won't tell anyone why. This is the strange way Bhishma's vow begins: not with Bhishma, but with his father saying no. And the no is honorable. Shantanu won't disinherit his son for his own wish. But look at what he does with the no. He doesn't let it settle. He keeps the refusal and the longing side by side, and carries both in silence. Nobody in the palace knows what's wrong. The king is keeping faith with one son and grieving for one woman at the same time. And the person who will notice first is the son the no was meant to protect. The young woman's own story is still to come. For now she's only the fisherman's daughter, and a condition the king won't meet.

Neither has to win right now. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's vow. It begins with a king's refusal: he won't give his son's crown away, even for the woman he wants.
Your line: the no and the longing, side by side. Today, if you're carrying a quiet no that still hurts, name it to one person you trust. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: Bhishma's vow
711.carry: a true reason, not the whole one
711.howItsDone: In some Hindu families, caring for aging parents and honoring their wishes is treated as a child's duty, and Bhishma's devotion to his father is held up in retellings as an example of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma's vow began without Bhishma: a scent by the Yamuna, a fisherman's condition, and a king who said no and kept longing — the no and the longing, side by side. Who did you tell about a quiet no? Day seven hundred eleven.
screen: `THE NO AND THE LONGING, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Devavrata, the heir, has watched his father grow quiet and pale, sitting lost in thought, and he can't find a reason for it anywhere. The kingdom is at peace, and nothing is missing that he can see. So the son does something that takes a little nerve with a king. He stands before him and asks straight out: everything in the kingdom is going well, so why are you grieving? And Shantanu answers him. Just not completely.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU GRIEVING?` → `THE SON ASKS STRAIGHT OUT.` → `THE FATHER ANSWERS, PARTLY.`

segments.voice: Here is Shantanu's answer, in the text's sense. You are my only son. And the wise say that a man with one son is like a man with none. You're a warrior, always among weapons. If you fell in battle, what would become of our line? That's what troubles me. Every word of it is something the king could mean. In the world of the poem, a royal line resting on one young warrior is a real worry. But it isn't the reason he's grieving, and the text lets us see that. Shantanu is dressing a private longing in a public concern. He can't say, I want a woman whose father demands your crown. So he says, I'm afraid for the family. Devavrata hears it, and he doesn't argue. He thinks it over, and then he goes to someone who would know: an old minister, devoted to his father. He asks him what's really behind the king's grief. And the old man tells him: the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna, and her father's condition, that her son must be king. Now Devavrata knows what his father couldn't say. And notice what he does not do. He doesn't confront his father with it. He doesn't sulk about a crown he might lose. He listens to the half answer, quietly finds the other half, and starts to think about what he can do. A true reason, not the whole one. The vow to come rests on a son who heard the difference.

segments.voice: The heir to the throne comes to a fisherman's door, and he doesn't come alone. Devavrata brings old chiefs of the warrior class with him, elders whose word carries weight. He has come on his father's errand: to ask for the fisherman's daughter as a bride for the king. The fisherman receives them with honor. And then, politely, carefully, with all those elders listening, he tells the prince exactly what's wrong with the match.
screen: `A PRINCE AT A FISHERMAN'S DOOR.` → `ELDERS AS WITNESSES.` → `WHAT'S WRONG WITH THE MATCH.`

segments.voice: The fisherman starts with praise. This match, he says, is one anyone would want; to turn it down would be foolish. He has no quarrel with the king. But there is one fault, and he names it: a rival. Whoever has you as a rival, he tells Devavrata, god or demon, can never live happily for long. That's a bold thing to say. A fisherman, speaking to a warrior prince, the king's own heir, in front of witnesses, is saying, in effect: the problem is you. Your strength. Your claim. Any grandson of his would grow up in that shadow. And Devavrata doesn't argue. He doesn't say he'd never harm a child, or ask to be trusted. He answers the problem by removing it. Hear my vow, he says, before all these chiefs. The son born of her will be our king. I give up the throne. The place he gives up is heir apparent, yuvaraja, the one his father gave him when he brought him home from the river. A few days ago in our reading, we watched Shantanu make him heir. Now, for his father's happiness, he hands it away to a brother who isn't even born. Notice where he speaks it. Not in private, not to his father, but in a fisherman's house, before elders who can hold him to it. A vow with witnesses is hard to take back, and he seems to want it that way. And the fisherman listens, and thanks him. Then he says there's one more thing he's worried about. That's tomorrow.

713.title: Bhishma's vow
713.carry: what was foretold, and what he chose
713.howItsDone: Brahmacharya, celibacy and self-restraint, is the discipline of the student stage of life in Hindu tradition, and some Hindu monks and renunciants keep it for life.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Bhishma's vow: a fisherman named the problem, and before the elders Devavrata gave up the throne — a vow with witnesses is hard to take back. What small thing did you give up for someone? Day seven hundred thirteen.

The fisherman is a careful man. He has just heard the heir to the throne give up his crown, in front of witnesses, for a grandson who isn't born yet. He believes him. He says so. And then he keeps thinking, out loud, while the elders listen. You'll keep your word, he says. But you'll have sons one day. Will they keep it? A promise is only as strong as the people who inherit it.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN BELIEVES HIM.` → `BUT WHAT ABOUT YOUR SONS?` → `WHO INHERITS A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: Devavrata answers him before the chiefs. I've already given up the kingdom, he says. Now I'll settle the matter of my children. From today, I take up brahmacharya, a vow of celibacy, for the rest of my life. And then he adds, in the text's sense: even if I die without a son, I'll still reach the heavenly worlds. The fisherman is shaken; the text says the hair on his body stood on end. I give her, he says. And then the sky answers. Gods, celestial dancers and sages rain flowers down on Devavrata's head, and they cry out a name. This one is Bhishma. In Ganguli's English the name is glossed, in brackets, with one word: terrible. He was born Devavrata. From this moment the story calls him Bhishma, after the thing he promised. Now reach back to the Vasus. When Ganga agreed to be their mother, the Vasus said the son who stayed on earth would have no children. Vasishtha said the same in his curse. It was foretold twice. And here, at a fisherman's house, nobody forces it on him. Devavrata chooses it, freely, out loud, for his father's happiness. What was foretold and what was chosen land on the same spot. The text doesn't tell us which matters more. It lets both be true at once: a life shaped long before he was born, and a man who stands up and makes it his own.

714.title: Bhishma's vow
714.carry: a vow is also a shape for a life
714.howItsDone: Some Hindus address goddesses, elders and respected women as Mata or Ma, mother, a word of honor as well as of kinship.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Bhishma's vow: a lifelong vow of celibacy, flowers from the sky, and a new name, Bhishma — what was foretold, and what he chose. What small promise did you keep all the way? Day seven hundred fourteen.

The fisherman has given his consent, before the old chiefs who came with the prince. The flowers have stopped falling. The elders have heard everything. And the young prince turns to the fisherman's daughter, the woman he has just won as a bride for his father, and speaks to her as her son. Mother, he says, get into my chariot, and let's go home. With one word, the vow becomes something you can see.
screen: `ONE WORD: MOTHER.` → `GET INTO MY CHARIOT.` → `LET'S GO HOME.`

segments.voice: He doesn't send her with servants. He helps her into his own chariot and takes her himself, to Hastinapura, the Kuru capital. And when they arrive, he goes to his father and tells him all of it: the condition, the throne, the vow. The text says the kings who heard what he had done praised it, and they said it too: he is truly Bhishma. So the name the sky gave him is repeated on earth. Notice what that word mother does. Up to now the vow has been all about what he gives up: a crown, a marriage, sons. With one word it becomes about what he takes on. A stepmother he chose for his father. A place in a family that will grow around him and never through him. A vow is a refusal, and it's also a shape for a life, and he steps into the shape at once.
